title: String Methods
intro: A **method** is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot: `name.upper()`. String methods never change the original string — they return a **new** one, so store the result.

questions.prompt: `strip()` removes spaces at both ends, `lower()` and `upper()` change case, and `replace(old, new)` swaps text. `split()` breaks text into a **list** of pieces (lists come in module 6) and `join()` glues pieces back together.
questions.exampleCode:
raw = "  Hello World  "
print(raw.strip())
print(raw.lower())
print(raw.replace("World", "Python"))
print("a,b,c".split(","))
print("-".join(["x", "y", "z"]))
questions.explanation: Chain methods to do several steps at once: `raw.strip().lower()`.

questions.prompt: `email` was typed with stray spaces and mixed case. Store a cleaned version in `clean`: no spaces at the ends, all lowercase.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert clean == email.strip().lower(), 'clean should have no outer spaces and be all lowercase.'

questions.explanation: Normalising text before comparing it avoids duplicates like `Ana@x.com` and `ana@x.com`.

questions.hint: `find` gives the index of the first match.
questions.explanation: There are three `a`s, and the first `n` is at index 2.

questions.prompt: `title` holds a book title in lowercase. Store it with each word capitalised in `nice`.
questions.setupCode: title = "the old man and the sea"

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert nice == title.title(), 'nice should have a capital letter at the start of every word.'

questions.hint: There's a method named after what you want.
questions.explanation: `title()` capitalises the first letter of every word.
`startswith` and `endswith` return booleans — handy for checking file types.

questions.prompt: `name` should end up as `sam` with no spaces, but the spaces are still there. Fix it.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert name == 'sam', 'name should be sam with no spaces.'

questions.hint: String methods return a new string. Where does that result go?
questions.explanation: Strings can't be changed in place, so store the result back in the variable.

questions.prompt: Replace every `tea` with `coffee` in `sentence` (keep the capital in `Tea` → `Coffee`). Store the result in `updated`.
questions.setupCode: sentence = "I love tea. Tea is great in the morning."

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert updated == sentence.replace('tea', 'coffee').replace('Tea', 'Coffee'), 'Replace tea with coffee and Tea with Coffee.'

questions.hint: `replace` is case-sensitive, so you need two calls.
questions.explanation: Chaining two `replace` calls handles both spellings.

questions.prompt: Fill in the method so `colours` holds the three separate words.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert colours == ['red', 'green', 'blue'], 'colours should be the three separate words.'
tests.message: colours should hold red, green and blue.

questions.hint: Which method breaks text at spaces?
questions.explanation: With no argument, `split()` breaks at any run of spaces.

questions.prompt: `parts` holds the pieces of a date. Join them with `/` into `date`, for example `2026/10/29`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert date == '/'.join(parts), 'date should be the parts joined with /.'

questions.hint: The separator goes before the dot: `"/".join(…)`.
questions.explanation: `join` is called on the glue, not on the pieces.

questions.prompt: Usernames are stored without spaces or `@`, in lowercase. Clean `raw` into `username`, then store in `long_enough` whether it has at least 3 characters.

tests.name: username
tests.code: assert username == raw.strip().replace('@', '').lower(), 'username should have no outer spaces, no @, and be lowercase.'

tests.name: length
tests.code: assert long_enough == (len(username) >= 3), 'long_enough should be True when username has 3 or more characters.'

questions.explanation: Cleaning input step by step is one of the most common real-world string jobs.
